Double Slit Experiment

i
About the Simulation

In Young's double-slit experiment a single source lights two narrow slits, so the two slits are coherent. Their waves overlap on the screen and add — giving a row of bright and dark fringes.

Wave prediction (green): the two path amplitudes are added first and the sum is then squared — written |ψ₁ + ψ₂|². Bright where the path difference Δ = d sin θ equals mλ; dark where Δ = (m + ½)λ. On the axis both amplitudes are a, so they add to 2a and the central intensity is 4I₀ — hence the axis label I / 4I₀. Close one slit and the same curve drops to I₀, a quarter as tall.

Classical (orange): a broad spray of bullets hits the barrier; those that get through either slit land in two smooth lobes that simply add, P₁ + P₂ — no cancellation anywhere. Some screen positions get less with two slits open than the bullets picture allows: that is destructive interference.

Scale — read this: to make the wave visible, this bench runs at nanometre scale, d ≈ 3λ and L only a few times d. The angles are therefore large, so the maxima are equally spaced in sin θ but spread out in x as the order m rises. The familiar classroom result β = λD/d is the small-angle (sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ) limit of the same condition — push Screen Distance L to 8000 nm to get within a few percent of it.

Close a slit: use the S1/S2 buttons for the one-slit comparison. Raising Slit Width a (or lowering λ) narrows the single-slit envelope until its sinc² zeros bite into the fringes — that is concept C215, single-slit diffraction.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Orient yourself

A point source emits light of one wavelength λ. A barrier with two narrow slits, S1 and S2, stands between it and a detection screen. The expanding rings are the wavefronts.

The screen is blank — nothing is being recorded yet.

2 · Predict — the pattern

Both slits are open, the screen is blank and firing is paused so you can commit. After thousands of one-at-a-time arrivals, what builds up on the screen?

3 · Observe — dot by dot

Let it run — the chart now tracks the detections.

Where do the dark gaps sit — and does any single dot seem to "know" about them?

4 · Resolve — interference

Each arrival's landing probability comes from both slit paths interfering — the green curve the detections are filling. The two paths differ in length by Δ = d sin θ.

Bright where Δ = mλ, so the paths arrive in phase; dark where Δ = (m + ½)λ and they cancel.

5 · Predict — close one slit

Suppose slit S2 is closed, leaving one. What does the pattern become?

6 · Observe — one slit

S2 is closed and the screen is cleared. Run it again.

Where did the dark gaps go — and how tall is the curve now against the two-slit one you just saw?

7 · Resolve — one path

One open path → a smooth mound, one quarter as tall on the axis. Two equal amplitudes a add there to 2a, so the two-slit centre is 4I₀, not 2I₀ — the light is redistributed, not created. With one slit there is nothing to cancel against, so no bands.

8 · Extend — bullets vs waves

Both slits are open again, and the classical bullets prediction P₁+P₂ (dashed orange) is now drawn beside the wave prediction (green).

Find the positions where the green curve falls to zero while the orange one is still high — places that get less light with two slits open than bullets would give. No adding of separate one-slit patterns can do that.

Slit Control

Close one slit and the bands vanish, leaving one smooth mound a quarter as tall — two slits give 2a on the axis, so 4I₀. To make the single-slit spreading (diffraction) bite, raise Slit Width a or lower λ until a/λ > 2. With both slits open, look for the positions where the wave curve reaches zero — light from two paths cancelling.

Double Slit Experiment

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Light of one colour from a point source reaches a barrier with two narrow slits. A detection screen behind the barrier records where each arrival lands, one at a time, and a chart tracks the totals against two predictions.

What you'll learn

  • How the paths from the two slits to one point on the screen differ, and why that decides what lands there.
  • How slit separation d, wavelength λ and screen distance L set where light lands.
  • What changes when you close a slit, widen the slits, or switch to the classical bullet picture.
The apparatus: source, barrier with slits S1 and S2 a distance d apart, and a screen a distance L behind the barrier.

What's on screen

  • The 3D bench: the source and its expanding wavefronts, the barrier with S1 and S2, and the detection screen where each arrival leaves a dot.
  • Blue bars on the chart: where the arrivals have landed so far.
  • Green line: the wave prediction. A dashed orange line, when it is switched on, is the classical bullet prediction.
See itStart from the default setup and let it run. Watch for: wavefronts spreading from the source, and dots arriving on the screen one at a time.

Changing any slider clears the screen and starts the count again. The screen is a fixed 8000 nm wide, so the centre is at 0 and the edges are at ±4000 nm.

03

Light from the two slits adds, so each point on the screen depends on the path difference

One source lights both slits, so the waves leave S1 and S2 in step. At a point on the screen, the light from S2 has travelled a different distance from the light from S1. For a distant screen, at angle θ from the axis, that path difference is Δ = d sin θ. The two waves arrive in step when Δ is a whole number of wavelengths, and out of step when it is a half-odd number:

bright: d sin θ = mλ dark: d sin θ = (m + ½)λ
I = 4I₀ cos²(πΔ/λ)
m = 0, ±1, ±2, … I₀ is the intensity one slit gives on its own.
  • On the axis Δ = 0, so the waves always arrive in step there.
  • The chart's vertical axis is I / 4I₀, so the brightest points read 1.
See itRun the default setup for a while. Watch for: arrivals piling up in some places and leaving gaps in others, following the green curve.
04

The bands land where sin θ = mλ/d, and the classroom width β = λD/d holds only for small angles

A band at angle θ lands at x = L tan θ from the centre. Since tan θ grows faster than sin θ, the bands spread out as m rises. At the default setting:

Order msin θ = mλ/dθx = L tan θIn the sim
10.3319.2°1390 nm1414 nm
20.6641.0°3480 nm3518 nm

The sim uses the exact path lengths from each slit, so its bands sit a little farther out, within 2%. A third band would need sin θ = 0.98 and falls far off the screen. A smaller d or a longer λ raises sin θ and pushes bands outward. If d is smaller than λ there is no m = 1 band.

For small angles x ≈ mλL/d, so neighbouring bands are equally wide: β = λL/d, written λD/d in textbooks. Here the angles are large, and λL/d = 1313 nm is about 7% below the sim's 1414 nm. Doubling L nearly doubles the distances but leaves the error near 6%, because the angle depends on λ/d, not L.

d

This slider moves the sim too. It uses the current λ and L.

See itHalve the slit separation to d = 800 nm. Watch for: the bands moving far apart, so that only three fit on the screen.
See itDouble the screen distance to L = 8000 nm. Watch for: the pattern stretched to about twice the width, with the second band pushed off the screen.
05

Closing one slit leaves a smooth mound a quarter as tall as the two-slit peak

With S2 closed only one path remains, so there is nothing to cancel against. The curve becomes one smooth mound centred behind the open slit, with no gaps in it.

With both slits open, the two amplitudes on the axis add to 2a, so the intensity there is (2a)² = 4I₀. One slit gives only I₀. So the two-slit peak is four times the one-slit peak, not twice. The light is redistributed, not created: averaged over many bands, two slits give 2I₀, twice what one slit gives, as energy conservation requires.

  • The chart plots I / 4I₀, so the one-slit mound reads about 0.25 against 1 for the two-slit peak.
  • The sim never lets both slits close at once.
See itClose slit S2 and run again. Watch for: the gaps gone, and the green curve down at about a quarter of its earlier height.
06

Adding bullet counts gives two smooth lobes, but adding waves can cancel

If the arrivals were bullets, each would pass through one slit and land in a lobe behind it. The total would be P₁ + P₂, with no cancellation. Classical Pattern draws it as the dashed orange curve. Its lobes lie on straight lines from the source through each slit, at about ±1690 nm at the default setting. Its curve is close to zero on the axis, where the wave curve peaks at 1.

The wave curve adds the amplitudes first and squares afterwards: |ψ₁ + ψ₂|², not |ψ₁|² + |ψ₂|². It reaches zero at places such as ±680 nm and ±2300 nm, where P₁ + P₂ is still above zero. Bullets have no wavelength, so the wavelength slider switches off in this mode.

See itSwitch on Classical Pattern. Watch for: the orange curve as two separate lobes with almost nothing between them, while the green curve peaks in the middle.
07

A wider slit narrows the envelope and can remove whole bands

Each slit also spreads light by diffraction. This multiplies the bands by a broad envelope, sinc²β with β = π a sin θ / λ. A narrow slit gives a nearly flat envelope: at the default a = 200 nm the first and second bands read 0.95 and 0.81 of the centre. A wider slit, or a shorter λ, narrows it.

The envelope first reaches zero at sin θ = λ/a. A band that falls there is missing. For d = 1000 nm, a = 500 nm and λ = 300 nm, the second band would be at sin θ = 0.60, exactly where the envelope is zero. The first band survives at about 0.40 of the centre.

See itSet d = 1000 nm, a = 500 nm and λ = 300 nm. Watch for: a bright centre, a dimmer band each side, and no band where the second would sit, at about ±3000 nm.
08

Where it matters

  • Measuring a wavelength. Young's experiment of the early 1800s turned a measured band width, with d and the screen distance known, into a number for the wavelength of light: λ = βd/D.
  • Diffraction gratings. Many equally spaced slits obey the same condition, d sin θ = mλ, but with much sharper bright lines. Spectrometers use them to split light by colour.
  • Radio antennas. Two aerials fed in step send strong signal in some directions and weak in others, which is how some broadcast towers aim their coverage.
09

Summary

In one line. Two slits give two paths, and the difference between their lengths decides what reaches each point of the screen.

Key points

  • Bright where d sin θ = mλ, dark where d sin θ = (m + ½)λ. A band lands at x = L tan θ.
  • β = λL/d holds for small angles only. It is 7% low at the default.
  • One slit gives a mound of height I₀. Two slits give 4I₀ on the axis.
  • Waves add amplitudes then square. Bullets add probabilities.

Common mix-ups

  • "Two slits give twice the light on the axis." They give four times one slit's. The average over the pattern is twice.
  • "The bands are equally spaced on the screen." They are equal in sin θ. On the screen, equal spacing holds only for small angles.
  • "A dark gap is a shadow." Light from both slits reaches it, and the two waves cancel.

Things to try on your own

  • Set λ to 650 nm and check that the second band leaves the screen, so that three bands remain.
  • Close S2 and check that the curve drops to about a quarter of its two-slit height.
